title: “I Still Hear the Voices”: Wedding Guests Recall Horror of U.S. Bombing in Southern Iran
author: Peiman Salehi

TEHRAN, Iran--Hundreds of guests had gathered in two family homes in Kuhestak,
a coastal village in Iran's southern Hormozgan province near the Strait of
Hormuz, for a wedding celebration on Tuesday night when the missiles struck.

"I still hear the voices of the women who were ululating, and then suddenly
the roof of the living room and the walls came down on us," Zeinab Mallahi, a
guest at the wedding, told Drop Site News. "That sound follows me from night
into day and from day into night."

A projectile tore through the roof of one of the homes, leaving a crater
roughly 1.5 meters deep in the floor. Another struck a date palm, sending it
crashing into a wall. People began screaming and "running everywhere," she
recalled. "It was something I had only seen in movies. I had never seen a
missile. I had never seen shrapnel. I didn't understand what was happening."

Four people were killed instantly: Four-year-old Amir Ali Karimi, 16-year old
Mohammad Mallahi, 43-year-old Kolsoom Mallahi Nezhadnia, and 50-year-old
Zarkhatoun Taheri. Two days later, 22-year-old Asieh Molaeinezhad, who had
been critically wounded and placed in intensive care, died, bringing the death
toll to five. At least 60 others were wounded.

On August 30, the U.S. began bombing Iran again, with attacks concentrated in
the south of the country, after both sides had withheld strikes for weeks.
Iranian authorities said at least[ 14
others](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cj06q4ynpmjo) were killed in strikes
across Iran that night. Tehran responded by launching attacks at U.S. targets
in Jordan, Kuwait, Iraq, and Bahrain.

Ali Mallahi, a local fisherman and the father of the bride, told Drop Site
that at least 350 people had gathered to celebrate his daughter Maryam's
wedding when his house was struck.

"I really don't know what to say," Mallahi told Drop Site. "This happened in a
completely residential area. There were no military facilities around the
house."

As is typical of weddings in Hormozgan, the men and women were gathered in
separate family homes separated by less than a hundred meters. Mallahi was
with the men at his cousin Mohammad Rasoul's house, while the women had
assembled at his own. The explosion came without warning.

"My first thought was that a gas cylinder had exploded in my house," Mallahi
said. He rushed to check on the women, hearing a second and third explosion as
he got there. "When I arrived, everybody was running in different directions."

He continued, "For a moment I just froze. I didn't know what had happened. I
asked myself, did they really fire a missile at my house? What happened to my
daughter's wedding? What happened to my guests? My children, my wife,
everyone?"

Eight people were admitted to a hospital in Sirik, while six others were
placed in intensive care at the Hazrat Abolfazl Hospital in Minab. A further
26 patients were admitted to the hospital's surgical wards, according to
Pezhman Shahrokhi, a local health official. Of the six patients in intensive
care, one was in critical condition and had been intubated. A total of 36
patients were later discharged after receiving diagnostic and specialized
treatment.

U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM)[
described](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PUBLIC-
RELEASES/Article/4588389/centcom-completes-strikes-on-irgc-targets-in-iran/)
the September 1 wave of strikes in southern Iran as targeting the "air-defense
sites, radar systems, and maritime assets" of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard
Corps. On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance claimed the U.S. was investigating
the incident but added that he was "extremely skeptical" of the reports around
the attack. "What I can say with 100% confidence is that unlike [Iran], the
United States never targets civilians in combat. We never will do that. We
never have done that, and unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen,"
he said at a White House press briefing.

A Reuters [investigation](https://www.reuters.com/investigations/deadly-
strike-iranian-wedding-was-likely-direct-hit-by-us-munition-
analysis-2026-09-03/) found that the wedding bombing was likely a direct hit
by a U.S. munition and not a ricochet off another target.

"None of us had anything to do with politics. I don't know international law,
but I know what happened here is not right," Mallahi said. "America is
certainly responsible. My house was in a completely residential area. I don't
know what has happened to my life. My daughter's wedding was left unfinished.
My relatives are in the hospital. Even my sister has to undergo surgery
because of her injuries."

Hundreds gathered for the funeral on Thursday of the four victims killed on
the day of the attack, including mourners, relatives, military, and civilian
officials, according to state media.

"I feel ashamed in front of my guests now," Mallahi said. "They were supposed
to come here and be with us on my daughter's happy night. But now, whenever I
see them, I think I will lower my head. They came here because of us, and some
of them lost their children or their relatives."

More than 3,000 Iranians[ have been
killed](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/more-than-3000-iranians-
killed-during-war-medical-body-says-2026-04-09/) since the U.S. and Israel
launched the war on February 28, according to Iranian authorities, including
more than 50 during a 60-day truce before fighting resumed in July.

Mostafa Taheri, a Red Crescent emergency worker, told Drop Site his team
reached the site five minutes after receiving a report of the attack. They
were already on alert because of U.S. strikes the previous night.

"What I saw was happiness and grief existing in the same place," Taheri
recalled. "It still looked as if a celebration was taking place, the wedding
lights were still on."

Multiple wedding guests were still trapped beneath rubble when rescuers
arrived. Others had been injured by fragments. Taheri said it was the first
time he had encountered such a scene.

"We could hear the wounded screaming," he said. "We immediately started
finding people, moving the rubble and transferring the injured."

Residents and wedding guests helped rescuers clear debris and move casualties.
Some of the wounded had injuries to their hands, legs, and heads. Others were
bleeding heavily.

"I saw that a child had been killed," he said. "When I asked how old he was
and they told me he was four, it affected me deeply. Even now, two days later,
I am still thinking about him."
